Extortion
ex-tor'shun
n. (the wringing of money from another by force, threat, or the abuse of a position; named in the temple, in the prophets, and in the apostolic list of those to be put out)
From Latin extorquere, to twist out, from ex, out, and torquere, to twist — the same root as torture. The Hebrew at Ezekiel 22:12 is osheq, oppression; the Greek at Matthew 23:25 is harpage, plunder or seizure.

Biblical Definition

Extortion is theft carried out under colour of right, and Scripture is unsparing with it. Ezekiel puts it in the indictment of Jerusalem: “In thee have they taken gifts to shed blood; thou hast taken usury and increase, and thou hast greedily gained of thy neighbours by extortion, and hast forgotten me, saith the Lord GOD” (Ezekiel 22:12). The closing clause is the diagnosis — the forgetting of God is what makes the wringing of a neighbour possible. Our Lord applies the same word to the religious leadership: “ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess” (Matthew 23:25). The Greek harpage is the violence of a bird of prey, and the woe is not that the Pharisees kept the outside clean but that the vessel they polished had been filled by plunder. The Pharisee in the temple thanks God he is not an extortioner (Luke 18:11) — and goes down to his house unjustified, which is the sharpest possible comment on self-assessment in this matter. Paul lists the extortioner among those with whom the church is not to eat (1 Corinthians 5:11), placing him beside the fornicator and the idolater as a subject of discipline.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines extortion as the taking of money by force or oppression, especially by an officer of justice under colour of his office.

expand to see more

EXTORTION, n. The act of extorting; the act or practice of wresting any thing from a person by force, duress, menaces, authority, or by any undue exercise of power.

2. In law, any oppression by color or pretense of right; particularly the taking of money by an officer, by color of his office, either where none is due, or more than is due.

3. Force or illegal compulsion by which any thing is taken from a person.

EXTORT, v.t. To draw from by force or compulsion; to wrest or wring from by physical force, by menace, duress, violence, authority, or by any illegal means.

EXTORTIONER, n. One who practices extortion.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 22:12 — "In thee have they taken gifts to shed blood; thou hast taken usury and increase, and thou hast greedily gained of thy neighbours by extortion, and hast forgotten me, saith the Lord GOD."

Matthew 23:25 — "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess."

Luke 18:11 — "The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican."

1 Corinthians 5:11 — "But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat."

Modern Corruption

Extortion is imagined as a crime of the alley, and Scripture aims it at respectable men using lawful position to wring their neighbours.

expand to see more

The popular picture of extortion is a threat delivered in a dark street. Webster's legal definition is closer to the biblical use: any oppression by color or pretense of right, and particularly the taking of money by an officer under colour of his office. Ezekiel is not describing gangsters but the princes, priests, and prophets of Jerusalem. Our Lord is not describing thieves but the men who tithed mint and anise. Extortion in Scripture is what men in authority do with the leverage their authority gives them, which is why it can coexist with a scrupulously clean exterior — and why the cup was full.

1 Corinthians 5:11 keeps the word from becoming an abstraction. The extortioner is listed among those a church must not sit down to eat with, and the list concerns men called brethren. This is the discipline the New Testament actually prescribes for a professing believer who wrings his neighbour, and it is almost never applied — partly because the sin is hard to see when it wears a contract, and partly because the men most able to commit it are often the men a congregation can least afford to lose. Luke 18:11 stands over the whole subject as a warning: the man most confident he is no extortioner went home unjustified.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew osheq, oppression or extortion — Ezekiel 22:12; Greek harpage, plunder — Matthew 23:25; harpax, a robber or extortioner — 1 Corinthians 5:11.

expand to see more

Hebrew osheq — oppression, extortion, gain wrung from another; Ezekiel 22:12 and Leviticus 6:4.

Greek harpage — the act of seizing, plunder; Matthew 23:25 and Luke 11:39, of the inside of the cup.

Greek harpax — ravenous, an extortioner; 1 Corinthians 5:11 and 6:10, and of wolves in Matthew 7:15.

Greek pleonektes — a covetous man, one who has more at another's cost; the companion term in Paul's lists.

Latin extorquere, to twist out — the root also of torture; the violence is in the word.

Usage

"“Gained of thy neighbours by extortion, and hast forgotten me” — the two clauses belong together."

"“Within they are full of extortion and excess” — a clean cup filled by plunder."

"“I am not as other men are, extortioners” — and he went down to his house unjustified."
